column2: The sequence is tending Jethro's flock, leading it toward the wilderness, then reaching Horeb. Priest of Midian describes Jethro, and this verse names Horeb without the familiar additional mountain-of-God formula.

The appearing subject is the Lord's angel; the flame is from the bush. The contrast between burning and not being consumed belongs to the narrated sight and is preserved without explaining its mechanism.
Moses resolves to turn aside and examine the great sight, particularly why the bush does not burn up. The question is his stated purpose, not a narrator's scientific explanation.

The Lord sees the approach and calls the name twice from the bush. Moses' response asks what it is; the inherited wording correctly avoids replacing it with the familiar Here I am from other textual traditions.
Two imperatives forbid further approach and require removal of footwear. The explanation identifies the standing place as holy ground; the spatial reference is to Moses' present location.

God identifies Himself through Moses' father and the three patriarchs. Moses turns his face away because he fears looking at God; the text gives both action and motive, rather than merely saying he covered his face.

The cognate seeing expression supports emphatic surely seen, followed by hearing the cry because of taskmasters and knowing the people's pain. The three perceptions remain distinct rather than being compressed to a general awareness.

Divine descent is directed toward rescue, bringing the people out of Egypt and bringing them into a good, spacious land flowing with milk and honey. The selected list includes Girgashites as well as the other six peoples; no name is removed to match another version.

The present arrival of Israel's cry is coupled with having seen Egyptian oppression. The repeated oppression wording reinforces the cause of intervention and does not supply an additional plague prediction.
The command sends Moses to Pharaoh, identified as Egypt's king, to bring the people out. The first-person possessive on My people and the explanatory sons of Israel retain their relationship.
Moses' self-question concerns both going to Pharaoh and bringing Israel out. It expresses inadequacy through a question, not a direct refusal or an added assertion that he lacks authority.

God's presence promise addresses Moses singularly; the subsequent serving of God at this mountain uses a plural verb for the delivered community. Ordinary English you permits both, but the number shift requires attention in fuller alignment.
The hypothetical approach to Israel introduces a question about the sender's name. Moses asks what he is to say to them; no divine name is supplied before the next verse's answer.

The selected Greek presents I am the One Who Is and then uses the same substantive expression as the sender. Preserve that formulation rather than importing a different Hebrew-based tense or a New Testament cross-reference into the translation.

The Lord title is connected with the patriarchal identification, everlasting name and generational memorial. Capitalization is editorial; the Greek title does not itself authorize inserting a Hebrew proper name.

Moses must gather the elders' council and announce the patriarchs' God. The emphatic visiting expression includes what has happened in Egypt; seen in the inherited English explicates the awkward coordination and remains a point for fuller syntax review.

The promise repeats ascent from affliction into the named peoples' land. All seven groups and the milk-and-honey image are retained; the repetition is part of the promised message, not disposable redundancy.

The elders listen and accompany Moses. The Hebrews' God has called them in this Greek reading, followed by a three-day journey and sacrifice; met with us would replace the selected verb's formulation.

Divine knowledge anticipates the king's refusal, with the strong-hand exception. The conditional qualification is retained; the statement should not be flattened into an unqualified prediction of permanent refusal.

The divine hand is stretched out to strike the Egyptians with wonders, after which Pharaoh releases the people. The temporal afterward is consequential to those acts, not an added separate stage of negotiation.
God gives this people favour before the Egyptians, and departure will not be empty-handed. The future negation concerns what they carry away, not a denial that anyone remains in Egypt.

Each woman asks her neighbour and fellow lodger for silver, gold and clothing; the goods are put on sons and daughters. The concluding plunder description must remain alongside asking, without an invented loan or repayment arrangement.

Moses raises prospective disbelief and refusal to heed his voice, then quotes the people's anticipated denial of the divine appearance. The selected opening includes his question about what to say; it is not merely a bare assertion of unbelief.
The Lord's question singles out the object in Moses' hand, answered as a staff. The short exchange should remain concrete and need not identify the staff's later symbolic role here.

The staff becomes a serpent after the command to throw it down, and Moses flees from it. Serpent follows this verse's noun; the different creature term in chapter 7 should not be silently standardized to it.
Moses is commanded to grasp the tail; he stretches out, takes hold and the object becomes a staff in his hand. The tail instruction and the final location are both relevant to the sign's reversal.
The purpose clause explains belief in the appearance of the Lord, God of the three patriarchs. It depends on the sign narrative rather than introducing a new divine appearance at this point.
The hand is placed in the bosom and emerges as snow. This Greek wording does not name leprosy in the verse, so no medical diagnosis is added to complete a familiar account.
The second insertion and withdrawal restores the hand to the colour of his flesh. The explicit colour comparison is preserved; healed would be a broader interpretive summary of the sign.
The two signs are distinguished as first and latter, and the Greek gives a voice to each sign. Retaining that personification preserves the connection between signs and the people's listening.
If both signs and Moses' voice fail to convince, river water is poured on dry land and becomes blood there. Both the double condition and the location of the transformation are maintained.

Moses' lack of ability extends over yesterday, the day before and the period since God began speaking. Weak voice and slow tongue distinguish his two descriptions without imposing a modern speech diagnosis.

The rhetorical questions move from giving a human mouth to hearing, sight and blindness, ending with God's identification. The adjacent hearing adjectives have overlapping ranges; the inherited distinction remains provisional pending specialist lexical review.
The divine promise is to open Moses' mouth and teach what he should say. Replacing open with the familiar be with would lose the selected Greek's verb and its link to the preceding mouth question.
Moses asks for another able person to be appointed. Able is expressed in the selected text; the request is stronger than simply send whom Thou wilt without the stated alternative person.

God's anger introduces Aaron the Levite, Moses' brother, who will speak to him and rejoice within himself at meeting him. The emphatic speaking construction should not automatically become an unqualified claim of eloquence.

Moses conveys God's words to Aaron, while God promises to open both men's mouths and teach them what to do. The shift to plural instruction is significant; the words are explicitly Mine in this reading.

Aaron serves as Moses' mouth to the people, while Moses has the things pertaining to God for Aaron. This expression should not be replaced with the more direct be God to him found in a different formulation.

The staff to be taken is expressly identified as the one changed into a serpent, and it is the instrument for the signs. The relative clause belongs to the selected Greek and is not an explanatory modern addition.
Moses asks Jethro to return to his brothers in Egypt and see whether they are still alive. Jethro's reply wishes health; the inherited expression avoids silently substituting peace.

The selected text first reports, after many days, the Egyptian king's death, then gives the Midian command. Those seeking Moses' life are plural and dead; their relationship to the one king is not specified by collapsing the clauses.

Moses takes his wife and children, places them on beasts of burden, and returns to Egypt with the staff from God. Both children and transport animals are plural; the verse does not specify a single donkey.

The wonders placed in Moses' hands are to be done before Pharaoh. God states that He will harden Pharaoh's heart, followed by emphatic refusal to release the people; this verse's assigned agency remains distinct from later formulations.

Israel is called God's firstborn son in the message to Pharaoh. The corporate singular image is retained without changing it to a plural firstborn population or adding an explanatory adoption doctrine.

The demand to release My people leads into service to God, then refusal and the threatened death of Pharaoh's firstborn. The collective people takes a singular serving verb, followed by plural them as the release object; English pronouns need not erase that shift.

The encounter at the lodging place explicitly names the Lord's angel as the assailant. The object him is not named in the clause; retain the pronoun and flag its referent rather than resolving the difficult episode through an inserted name.

Zipporah uses a stone, cuts her son's foreskin and falls at the feet, whose owner is not specified here. The selected utterance says the blood of her child's circumcision has ceased; bridegroom-of-blood language would harmonize to another textual form.

Departure from him follows the repeated cessation-of-blood declaration. Both pronouns and the causal connection to her words require cautious retention; the narration does not explicitly identify each referent.
Aaron is sent into the wilderness, meets Moses at God's mountain, and the brothers kiss one another. The reciprocal plural action is preserved rather than assigning the kiss to only one brother.

The relative pronoun after all the Lord's words is masculine accusative plural, matching words as what was sent. The inherited with which He had sent him introduces a personal object and instrumental relation not expressed here; propose words the Lord had sent, leaving the separate commanded-signs clause intact.

Moses and Aaron together gather the elders' council of the sons of Israel. The collective council expression is retained without implying that the whole population assembled in this particular action.
Aaron is the expressed subject of speaking and remains the grammatical subject of performing the signs before the people. Assigning the signs automatically to Moses would override this sequence.

The people believe and rejoice that God has visited and seen their affliction, then bow and worship. Rejoiced follows the selected reading; heard would import the more familiar alternative narrative wording.
The joint approach announces the Lord, Israel's God, and asks release for a wilderness festival. Hold a feast conveys the festival verb without narrowing it to eating a meal alone.

Pharaoh asks whose voice he should obey, denies knowing the Lord and refuses Israel's release. The opening pronoun remains tied to the divine speaker in the preceding demand; no different deity is introduced.

The Hebrews' God has called them, followed by a three-day journey and sacrifice. Death or slaughter are the feared encounters in this Greek reading, not the familiar alternative pair pestilence and sword.
Egypt's king accuses both men of turning his people from work and orders each to his own work. The distributive each prevents the command from being read only as a general policy statement.

Pharaoh comments on the people's numerousness and says let us not give them rest. The first-person plural deliberation is preserved; changing it to you make them rest would alter the selected grammar.
The royal order addresses both taskmasters and scribes. Scribes is retained as an administrative designation, with no assumption that they are modern clerical workers or identical to the taskmasters.

The passive prohibition ends the provision of straw and makes the people gather it themselves. As before idiomatically renders yesterday and the third day; the contrast is established practice versus the new burden.

The daily assigned brick quantity remains unchanged, and Pharaoh explains the religious request as idleness. The singular administrative you is followed by plural workers; his allegation is kept as his speech, not narrator judgment.
Heavier work and attention to it are contrasted with attention to empty words. The repeated attention verb supports the inherited parallelism and marks Pharaoh's dismissal of the request.
Taskmasters and scribes press the people and announce Pharaoh's first-person withdrawal of straw. The narration describes pressure, not merely the officials' physical departure.

The emphatic self-directed gathering command allows any place where straw can be found. The explanatory clause denies any reduction in the appointed quantity; it does not promise more time for gathering.
The population scatters throughout Egypt to gather stubble as a substitute source of straw. The two material nouns remain distinct rather than describing ordinary delivery of prepared straw.

The taskmasters demand completion of each day's due work under the former supply rate. The comparison explicitly invokes the period when straw was given, making the increased burden clear without commentary.

Israelite scribes appointed by Pharaoh's supervisors are flogged for deficient brick quotas. The passive punishment and the quoted accusation have different agents; the inherited asked is contextual English support for the ensuing speech.
The scribes enter and cry out to Pharaoh, calling themselves his household slaves. Their submissive designation is part of the petition and should not be softened into equal negotiating partners.

Their complaint contrasts absent straw with demanded bricks and completed flogging. The final future accusation says Pharaoh will wrong his people; it is not a narrator's declaration that the workers are at fault.
Pharaoh repeats the idleness charge with both verb and noun, then attributes the sacrifice request to it. The inherited You are idle; you are idlers preserves that emphatic repetition.
The command to work is accompanied by both denied straw and required brick delivery. The future obligations are not conditional on a successful petition or restored supplies.

The scribes recognize their distress, followed by the unreduced daily-brick wording. The Greek saying construction leaves its discourse relation awkward; retain the inherited presentation provisionally rather than inventing an explicit new speaker.
The departing officials meet Moses and Aaron, who are themselves coming to meet them. The two movements and the Pharaoh departure belong to different participants and are kept clear in English.

They invoke God's seeing and judging, then describe their odour as made loathsome before Pharaoh and his attendants. The sword is placed in Pharaoh's hands; the metaphor conveys mortal danger without adding an actual execution order.

Moses turns to the Lord with two accusatory questions about afflicting this people and sending him. Direct singular divine address follows the standard's Thou forms while preserving the questions' force.
Moses links his visit in God's name with Pharaoh's subsequent oppression and the lack of deliverance. The two agents remain distinct: Pharaoh afflicted, while God is addressed as not having rescued.
God predicts Pharaoh's release and expulsion under a mighty hand and uplifted arm. These two images are retained in the selected sequence instead of repeating mighty hand for both clauses.
The short first-person identification uses the title Lord. English supplies the ordinary copula; no Hebrew proper-name expansion is warranted by this Greek clause alone.
The patriarchal appearance is described as being their God, followed by not revealing the name Lord. This wording must not be replaced by an Almighty title absent from the selected running text.

The established covenant promises Canaanite land and repeats the patriarchs' sojourning there. The English keeps both the place and their resident-foreigner status without introducing ownership before the promise.

God hears Israel's groaning under Egyptian enslavement and remembers your covenant. The second-person possessive is the selected reading; silently regularizing it to My covenant would obscure a source-specific detail.
The command to speak introduces release from domination, rescue from slavery and ransom with uplifted arm and great judgment. The singular judgment and the three deliverance verbs remain distinct.

God takes the people for Himself and promises to be their God, leading to recognition of the one who brought them out. The participle's completed presentation sits within future promises and need not be flattened to another future verb.

The stretched-out hand refers to the land promised to the three patriarchs, followed by giving it as an allotted inheritance. The inherited wording keeps the bodily image rather than inserting an unexpressed oath formula.
The failure to listen is attributed to discouragement and harsh work. The two causes describe the hearers' condition, not an added moral judgment that they reject God deliberately.
The renewed divine speech formula introduces the next verse's command. Retaining this short unit preserves the stored verse boundary rather than merging it into 6:11.
Moses must enter and address Pharaoh, Egypt's king, with Israel's departure as the aim. The command is singular to Moses; it does not yet restate Aaron's participation.

Moses reasons from Israel's not listening to Pharaoh's likely response and describes himself as without speech or eloquence. The speech adjective is not the uncircumcised-lips expression of another tradition; exact degree remains a lexical question.
The Lord addresses Moses and Aaron and charges them concerning Pharaoh for Israel's release. The selected running text does not insert an additional command directed toward Israel in this verse.

The genealogy begins with heads of ancestral houses and Reuben's four sons, identifying him as Israel's firstborn. Familiar inherited English name forms are retained provisionally; they are not claims of letter-for-letter Greek transliteration.

Six sons are listed for Simeon, with Shaul identified through a Phoenician mother. Phoenician is the selected Greek designation and should not be changed to Canaanite merely to match a familiar genealogy.
Levi's three sons are grouped by kindred and his lifespan is one hundred and thirty-seven years. The numeral belongs to Levi, not the sons collectively; no modernized numerical approximation is used.
The two Gershon descendants are followed by their ancestral-house description. Retention preserves the plural family units rather than making the closing phrase a third personal name.
Kohath has four named sons and lives one hundred and thirty years in the selected text. The figure is not harmonized to one hundred and thirty-three from another textual form.
Merari's two sons complete the summary of Levi's ancestral houses by kindreds. The concluding these refers to the listed family structure, not only a new otherwise unnamed pair.

Jochebed is the daughter of Amram's father's brother in this Greek text; Aaron, Moses and their sister Miriam are born to him. The lifespan is one hundred and thirty-two, and neither kinship nor number is harmonized elsewhere.
Izhar's three sons are separately named, without added offices or later narrative identifications. Stable inherited names are retained pending the shared name-authority review.
Uzziel's sons are two in this selected list. A third son known from another genealogy must not be supplied to complete a familiar pattern.
Elisheba is both Amminadab's daughter and Nahshon's sister, and the four sons belong to her marriage with Aaron. The two relational descriptions must remain attached to the wife rather than to Aaron.
Korah's three sons are followed by a generations summary. The plural ancestry formula is retained without importing later associations of the Korahites into the names.

Eleazar takes a wife from Putiel's daughters and she bears Phinehas. One of is necessary English for the Greek partitive construction; the concluding Levite heads are a genealogical summary, not additional children.

Aaron and Moses are identified as the recipients of God's exodus command, with Israel's force or host accompanying the departure. Forces preserves the collective organizational image without asserting a modern military formation.

The same two men speak to Pharaoh and bring Israel out, followed by their repeated identification. The summary's accomplished narrative perspective is retained even though the detailed deliverance story follows.
The temporal clause specifies the day of divine speech in Egypt and continues into the next stored unit. Its open syntax is intentional; it should not be given an invented independent main verb.

The Lord's identity precedes the command to repeat to Pharaoh everything being said to Moses. The breadth of the relative expression supports all that, without adding a separate demand for interpretation.

Moses again asks how Pharaoh will hear him, now using the weak-voiced description found earlier. Retain the lexical difference from without eloquence in 6:12 rather than standardizing both self-descriptions.

God appoints Moses as a god to Pharaoh and Aaron as Moses' prophet. The relational qualification to Pharaoh is essential; the statement should not become an unrestricted claim about Moses' divine nature.

Moses speaks the whole command to Aaron, who then speaks to Pharaoh for Israel's release. The first him is explained by this mediation structure rather than automatically identifying it with Pharaoh from the preceding verse.

God explicitly undertakes the hardening and multiplication of signs and wonders. Preserve both nouns and this verse's divine agency without imposing the same grammatical agency on every later heart statement.

Pharaoh will not listen to the plural you, and divine intervention brings Israel out with God's power and great vengeance. My belongs to power in this selected text, distinct from references to Israel's forces elsewhere.

All Egyptians will recognize the Lord through His outstretched hand and Israel's removal from among them. The final exodus action remains linked to the identity claim rather than becoming an unrelated promise.
The report names both Moses and Aaron and repeats that they did as commanded. The seemingly redundant closing so they did reflects the source's emphatic compliance formula.

The ages are eighty for Moses and eighty-three for Aaron. The final speaking verb is singular in the selected text, so inherited when he spoke is not silently changed to a plural even though both men feature in the encounter.
The Lord addresses both brothers before the conditional instructions. This shared address frames the subsequent shift to Moses' singular instruction to Aaron.

Pharaoh's possible request is for a sign or wonder; Moses then tells Aaron to cast the staff down before Pharaoh and his attendants. Dragon preserves the Greek creature term's difference from serpent in chapter 4, without asserting a modern zoological identification.
The brothers enter together, but Aaron is expressly the one who throws the staff. The transformation again uses the dragon term, preserving the event's link with the preceding instruction.
Pharaoh summons wise men and sorcerers, and the Egyptian enchanters imitate the act through sorceries. These overlapping descriptions are not merged into a single unqualified modern profession.

Each rival throws his own staff, which becomes a dragon; Aaron's staff swallows their staffs. The narrator returns to staff terminology for the swallowing, and that wording should not be replaced merely to regularize the image.

The heart grows strong and Pharaoh fails to listen, as the Lord said to the brothers. Strong retains the verb's distinction from heavy and hardened in nearby reports without claiming three entirely separate psychological states.

The Lord describes Pharaoh's heart as having become heavy, with refusal to release the people. The result-oriented formulation remains different from an explicit active statement that Pharaoh hardened himself.
Moses is to meet Pharaoh at the river bank in the morning, taking the staff that became a serpent. This verse uses serpent rather than the dragon noun in 7:9–12; preserve that lexical switch.

The divine commissioning message identifies the Hebrews' God and repeats the demand for wilderness service. The concluding until now marks the duration of Pharaoh's failure to listen, not a statement that he has already changed his mind.

The quoted divine declaration places the staff in My hand and announces the water's change into blood. Retain the first-person wording even though human agents carry out the action in the following narrative.
Fish death, river stench and inability to drink form a sequence of effects. The negative ability statement concerns river water, not a universal claim that no other possible water source exists.

Aaron is instructed over rivers, canals, marshes and standing water; the fulfillment extends to wood and stone. The latter nouns are left as written rather than silently supplying vessels or asserting a specific material explanation.

The brothers' obedience precedes a singular, unnamed agent raising and striking with the staff. The inherited he preserves the grammatical presentation; Aaron is contextually likely, but an explicit subject name would be interpretive.

The narration fulfills the fish, stench and drinking predictions and adds the land-wide blood report. Repeated river and land scopes are maintained rather than treating them as interchangeable descriptions.
The enchanters imitate by their sorceries; the heart is hardened and Pharaoh refuses to listen. The passive heart verb need not be assigned an explicit agent not named in this clause.
Pharaoh turns home and does not apply his mind even to this event. The focus is lack of attention, not an added statement that he scientifically disproved the sign.
All Egyptians dig around the river in order to drink, while inability to drink from the river is repeated. The text does not state in this verse whether those excavations succeeded.
Seven days are completed after the Lord strikes the river. This specifies an interval without independently defining the precise duration of every effect listed in the preceding account.
The next demand begins within chapter 7 in this numbering. It asks release for service to God; moving it into a conventional chapter 8 would break the repository's selected unit identity.

The refusal condition introduces frogs as the means of striking all Pharaoh's territory. Borders is the inherited territorial expression, not merely a claim about insects at Egypt's political frontier.

The river brings forth frogs into royal houses, bedrooms, beds, attendants' and people's houses, dough and ovens. Dough follows the actual material noun; replacing it with kneading bowls would add an unexpressed container.
The frogs rise onto Pharaoh, his attendants and his people. The repeated personal targets extend the preceding list of domestic locations and should not be collapsed to houses alone.
Moses is to direct Aaron to extend the staff by hand over the named waters and bring up frogs. Rivers, canals and marshes remain differentiated, matching the setting of the earlier water sign.

Aaron brings up frogs, followed by a collective singular frog in the covering clause. Natural English plural frogs conveys that collective without implying one enormous animal; the active and passive stages both remain.

Egyptian enchanters bring up frogs through sorceries in imitation. This reports what they do, without inventing an ability to remove the frogs which the next negotiation instead requests from the Lord.

Pharaoh asks prayer for himself and removal from himself and his people, then promises to release the people. The inherited them can point back to Egyptians; restore the explicit the people to preserve the Greek switch to the captive people who will sacrifice.

Moses gives Pharaoh the choice of prayer time for himself, attendants and people. Destruction away from their houses is limited by frogs remaining in the river; appointed timing and geographic exception are both explicit.

Pharaoh says tomorrow, and Moses accepts his word with the purpose of recognizing no other except the Lord. This reading is stronger in form than simply no one like the Lord and should not be normalized to that alternative.

Removal is promised from persons, houses and farmsteads, with the river exception repeated. The plural your houses broadens beyond Pharaoh's own residence, while the servants and people remain separately named.

The two men leave, but Moses alone cries to the Lord concerning the defined limit or appointment for frogs as Pharaoh arranged. Appointed limit is retained provisionally because the noun's precise temporal or boundary force needs fuller lexical review.
The Lord acts according to Moses' word and frogs die in houses, farmsteads and fields. The death report should not be paraphrased as all frogs simply retreating to the river.
The gathering is in heaps upon heaps, followed by land-wide stench. The repeated heap noun gives the image its scale and is preserved rather than reduced to a neutral cleanup statement.
Relief precedes the passive report that Pharaoh's heart became heavy and his refusal to listen. The clause does not expressly name Pharaoh as agent of the heart change, unlike 8:28.

Aaron's staff strikes earth or soil, producing gnats on humans and quadrupeds throughout Egypt. Gnats is a provisional traditional insect identification; no exact modern species is established by this focused comparison.

Aaron carries out the staff action, and the account repeats infestation of humans, quadrupeds and all the soil. The repeated locations emphasize breadth without adding a separate transformation mechanism beyond the wording.

The enchanters' attempted imitation fails; gnats nevertheless remain on people and animals. Tried appropriately expresses their doing with an unsuccessful purpose infinitive, rather than claiming successful production followed by an unrelated failure.

The enchanters identify the event as God's finger, but the passive hardening and refusal continue. The speaker attribution matters: this is their declaration within the narrative, not a newly inserted narrator explanation.

Moses must rise early and stand before Pharaoh as he goes to the water. The message again specifies wilderness service, preserving the location of the requested release rather than reducing it to worship anywhere in Egypt.

Refusal leads to dog-flies upon Pharaoh, attendants, people, houses and ground. The specific Greek insect designation is preserved provisionally without converting it to an unspecified swarm or claiming a precise modern species.

Goshen is to be treated exceptionally, without the flies, so Pharaoh knows the Lord as Lord of all the earth. Marvellously distinguish renders the extraordinary-treatment verb; the doubled Lord title belongs to the selected text.

A distinction is set between God's people and Pharaoh's people, and tomorrow is the sign's appointed time. The chosen text speaks of distinction rather than requiring a ransom term in the English here.

A multitude of flies enters Pharaoh's and his attendants' houses and all Egypt, ruining the land. The inherited plural renders the Greek collective insect noun naturally without weakening the magnitude.
Pharaoh offers sacrifice within the land rather than the requested wilderness departure. The location restriction is central to the negotiation and must remain explicit.

Moses rejects the offer because the sacrifices are abominations to the Egyptians and predicts stoning if performed before them. The English takes the genitive as what Egyptians regard as abhorrent; the precise cultural objects or reason are not supplied by this clause and remain unasserted.

The three-day wilderness journey and sacrifice are presented as what God told them. The statement retains both travel duration and conformity to the prior command, rather than treating the distance as a new bargaining invention.
Pharaoh promises departure but restricts distance and again asks prayer for himself. The permission is qualified, not an unconditional acceptance of every part of Moses' request.

Moses promises departure, prayer and tomorrow's removal, then prohibits another deception through withholding release. Again is warranted by the explicit recurrence construction; it is not added merely to heighten Pharaoh's culpability.
Moses leaves Pharaoh and prays to God. The short fulfillment clause preserves God as the title here, distinct from the Lord in the next verse's narration.
The Lord fulfills Moses' word and removes the flies from Pharaoh, attendants and people, leaving none. The emphatic complete-removal statement is not weakened to most of the swarm disappearing.
Here Pharaoh actively makes his own heart heavy and refuses to release the people. The explicit subject and active verb should remain distinct from the passive heart report in 8:11.
The renewed message identifies the Lord as the Hebrews' God and demands release for service. The repeated formula is retained as a fresh confrontation rather than omitted as already understood.

The refusal condition includes continued holding of God's people and leads into the next verse's threatened action. This stored unit remains syntactically open; no separate consequence is invented to close it.

The threatened hand falls on livestock in the fields, with horses, beasts of burden, camels, cattle and sheep enumerated. The closing exceedingly great death remains the selected expression rather than a named veterinary disease.

God will treat the two populations' animals differently, with none of Israel's possessions dying in this livestock context. The unusual final idiom is represented by nothing; it does not introduce a new kind of animal.

God appoints a limit or time and quotes tomorrow as the Lord's act on the land. The shift from God in narration to Lord in the announcement is preserved, rather than mechanically regularizing the titles.

The next-day fulfillment says all Egyptian livestock died and none of Israel's did. Preserve the absolute wording alongside the field scope in 9:3; later livestock references do not authorize silently changing all to some.

Pharaoh sees the absence of Israelite livestock deaths, yet his heart becomes heavy and release is withheld. The selected verb is seeing, not an inserted sending of investigators found in another account.
Both brothers are told to take full hands of furnace soot, but Moses is singled out to scatter it heavenward. Pharaoh's attendants are explicitly present along with Pharaoh in the instruction.

Soot becomes dust over Egypt, followed by sores and erupting blisters upon humans and quadrupeds. The repeated human-and-animal scope is preserved, without diagnosing the condition as a modern named disease.

The taking verb is singular, and Moses is then named as scattering the soot. The inherited he retains that grammar rather than converting the narrative to they on the strength of the earlier joint command.

The sorcerers cannot stand before Moses because they too have the sores; the effect is described throughout Egypt. The inability is explicitly linked to the physical affliction, not merely their failure to reproduce it.
The Lord actively hardens Pharaoh's heart, and Pharaoh does not listen. The closing comparison uses commanded in the selected reading; it need not be standardized to the said formula in other verses.
Moses again rises early and stands before Pharaoh with the Hebrews' God's demand. The repeated temporal command and service purpose keep this warning distinct from the preceding soot sign.

All divine blows or encounters are directed to Pharaoh's heart and to his attendants and people, so he recognizes no equal throughout the earth. The possessive coordination may extend heart to the others elliptically; retain the wording while flagging that scope for fuller syntax review.

The selected construction predicts stretching the hand, striking with death and erasure from the earth. It is not written as the counterfactual could have struck found in some familiar translations; preserve its future threat alongside the next verse.

Pharaoh has been preserved for displaying divine strength in him and proclamation of God's name everywhere. The passive preserved differs from raised up and should not be replaced to harmonize with a later quotation.

The selected edition punctuates an accusation, with still and therefore/yet, rather than a question. Propose Yet you still act against My people, refusing to let them go. This follows editorial punctuation, not proof that a Greek indicative cannot be a rhetorical question, and is not a claim of a manuscript variant. The uncommon verb's precise oppression or interference nuance remains unresolved.

The hail is timed to this hour tomorrow and described as unprecedented since Egypt's creation. The temporal extent follows the selected creation wording rather than substituting the nation formula that appears in 9:24.

Pharaoh is urged to gather livestock and everything in the field; humans and animals remaining outside when hail strikes will die. The warning combines outside location, failure to enter a house and exposure to hail, not an unqualified death sentence for all residents.
The representative attendant who fears the Lord's word gathers his livestock into houses. The selected wording mentions livestock here, and servants are not inserted from another version.

The contrasting attendant gives no mental heed and leaves livestock in the fields. The inherited wording retains the deliberative attention expression instead of reducing the contrast to simple ignorance of the warning.
Moses stretches his hand heavenward; hail is to fall upon people, livestock and every plant. The three targets are explicit, and the command says hand rather than requiring a staff in this verse.

Moses obeys, the Lord sends voices or thunder and hail, and fire runs across the land. Thunder is the contextual weather sense, while fire remains the narrative image without an added technical identification.

The fire flames within the hail, whose abundance is emphasized by a repeated intensifier. Very, very preserves that repetition; the unprecedented comparison now runs from the presence of a nation there.
The hail strikes humans, livestock and field vegetation, then shatters the field trees. Struck and shattered are distinct actions; the verse does not independently say every human struck died.
Goshen alone is excepted from hail, with Israel's presence given as its identifying description. The geographic exception is maintained alongside the broad all-Egypt statements.
Pharaoh's confession is qualified by this time, calls the Lord righteous and himself and his people ungodly. Retain the speaker's own contrast without narratorial certification of lasting repentance.

Pharaoh requests prayer for cessation of God's thunder, hail and fire, then promises release without further delay. Fire is explicitly part of this selected request and should not disappear in a shortened weather list.

Moses promises to spread his hands after leaving the city; thunder, hail and rain will cease to demonstrate the Lord's ownership of the earth. Rain here differs from the fire in Pharaoh's immediately preceding list.
Moses explicitly knows that Pharaoh and his attendants have not yet feared the Lord. Yet leaves the temporal qualification intact; it is not a claim that they can never do so.

Flax and barley are struck because barley is standing ready and flax is producing seed. The crop stages follow the chosen Greek wording; a different botanical stage should not be imported merely from a familiar English text.

Wheat and the grain provisionally called spelt escape because they are late. The precise ancient cereal identification requires specialist evidence; retain the inherited name without asserting a modern botanical species.

Moses leaves both Pharaoh and the city, spreads his hands, and the thunder and hail cease while rain no longer drips on the land. The fulfilled sequence retains the city's boundary and the three weather effects.

Seeing the cessation, Pharaoh sins again and actively makes his own heart and his attendants' hearts heavy. The genitive extension includes the attendants in the heart object, not as an independently stated plural subject.

The concluding heart verb is passive and release is refused, in accord with the Lord's word to Moses. Retention avoids flattening this summary into the active subject construction immediately before it.

God states that He hardened Pharaoh's and his attendants' hearts so these signs would come successively upon them. In succession renders the ordering adverb and is not an added theory about a fixed plague schedule.

The addressees become plural in the telling to children and grandchildren and in knowing the Lord. The description of mocking the Egyptians preserves the selected verb's force without softening it into generic acts.

The brothers deliver a question about refusal to show reverence, then the release demand. Reverence follows the Greek shame/respect construction; humble yourself is a possible contextual alternative, not an automatic replacement.

Refusal introduces many locusts at this hour tomorrow across Pharaoh's territory. The singular collective insect noun is naturally plural in English, while the quantity and precise announced timing remain.

The locusts cover the visible land and eat what the hail left, including growing trees. The switch between singular Pharaoh's inability to see and plural benefits left to you is implicit in ordinary English and warrants a number note in full alignment.

Houses of Pharaoh, attendants and all Egypt fill with an unprecedented infestation, measured against fathers and forefathers. Moses then turns away and exits; that action remains narration outside the quoted warning.

The attendants call the situation a hindrance and urge release of the human group, using the general people/persons noun. Propose people instead of men here, preserving its distinction from the explicit male-only noun in 10:11; the final question about knowing Egypt's destruction remains unchanged.

Unnamed people bring both brothers back, and Pharaoh asks exactly who is going. The repeated interrogative in Greek supports the specificity of the question; the passive English correctly leaves the returning agents unnamed.

Moses includes young men, elders, sons, daughters, sheep and cattle because this is their God's festival. Retain the demographic and livestock list rather than shortening it to everyone with their possessions.

Pharaoh's purported blessing is followed by a rhetorical challenge about sending their household group and a warning that evil lies before them. Household represents the collective dependents/baggage term contextually; the tone and exact force of the comparison remain matters for review.

Pharaoh restricts departure to adult men and claims that is what they seek. The unnamed agents then expel the brothers; neither a feminine collective nor all Israelites should replace the male noun in this restriction.

The extended hand calls up locusts to consume plants and tree fruit remaining after hail. The fruit wording is explicit here and is preserved alongside, rather than substituted for, the broader trees wording in 10:5.

Moses raises his staff heavenward and a south wind blows through day and night, carrying the locusts by morning. South is the selected direction; changing it to east would harmonize with another textual tradition.

The wind brings the collective locust infestation over Egypt, where it settles in unparalleled abundance. The comparison includes both the past and future; the inherited plural English does not alter the collective referent.
The land is covered and ruined, and remaining vegetation and tree fruit are eaten until nothing green remains. Ruined follows this Greek reading rather than silently replacing it with darkened.
Pharaoh urgently summons both brothers and confesses sin before their God and against them. The two prepositional relations are preserved, as is the plural human addressee.

The request asks the brothers to accept or bear his sin once more and pray for removal of this death. Forgive is a contextual rendering of the acceptance verb, not a claim that the Greek uses its usual release verb; the idiom remains flagged for lexical review.
Moses departs and prays to God, fulfilling the requested intercession. The verse does not itself announce a change in Pharaoh's disposition after prayer.

The Lord changes the wind to a strong one from the sea; it lifts the locusts into the Red Sea and leaves none. From the sea is retained rather than replacing the source's directional expression with west, and Red Sea follows its actual name.
The Lord again actively hardens Pharaoh's heart and Israel is not released. The stated agent remains divine in this clause; no broader theological causal explanation is added.

Moses is told to stretch his hand toward heaven for darkness that can be felt. The tactile description is preserved as the source's image, without supplying dust, fog or another proposed physical cause.
The event is described by darkness, gloom and tempest for three days. The threefold weather description belongs to the selected Greek and should not be reduced to darkness alone.

Three days is repeated for neither seeing a brother nor rising from bed, while Israel has light wherever dwelling. Bed follows the selected noun; the account's strong wording is retained without an invented explanation of daily activity.

Pharaoh summons both Moses and Aaron and allows their household to go while retaining sheep and cattle. The explicit Aaron and the family-versus-livestock distinction are preserved against a simplified account naming Moses alone.

Moses requires Pharaoh also to supply whole burnt offerings and sacrifices for their God. Both offering categories remain; the statement is a demand within the exchange, not a report that Pharaoh has already supplied them.

Their own livestock must accompany them, with not a hoof left, since the required service is not known until arrival. The hoof image expresses complete departure and should not be turned into an invented numerical quota of offerings.
Divine hardening is followed by Pharaoh's unwillingness to release them. The will verb makes refusal explicit and is not merely a prediction that departure fails for unspecified practical reasons.
Pharaoh orders Moses away, warns against another appearance and threatens death on that day. Ordinary singular you is retained for this personal warning, without divine-address archaic forms.

Moses affirms Pharaoh's statement and says he will no longer appear before his face. The inherited appearance wording preserves the Greek passive presentation; it does not promise that Moses will never see any part of Pharaoh again.

One further plague leads to release and emphatic expulsion with everything. The cognate expulsion expression supports altogether, while with everything reflects the separate accompaniment phrase; neither should imply only the male workers may leave.

The people are to hear the instruction secretly, and men and women ask their corresponding neighbours for silver, gold and clothing. Secretly and clothing are present in this Greek reading and must not be omitted to match another version.

Divine favour is followed by the Egyptians' lending and Moses' greatness before Egyptians, Pharaoh and all attendants. Lending is the selected verb here, unlike a mere request in 3:22; no repayment arrangement is inferred beyond it.
Moses introduces a divine declaration of entry into Egypt around midnight. About preserves the approximate temporal preposition; it need not be replaced by the precise narrative midnight of 12:29.

The death range extends from Pharaoh's firstborn to the female slave's at the mill and livestock firstborn. The throne relative grammatically relates to Pharaoh; the mill worker is not substituted for the captive woman in the later fulfillment wording.
The great cry is unprecedented and will not recur in this form. Both backward and forward comparisons remain, without shortening the statement to an ordinary loud outcry.

No dog growls with its tongue against Israel, from humans to animals, demonstrating extraordinary divine distinction. The unusual tongue image is retained; bark would be a contextual simplification requiring an explicit stylistic decision.

Moses predicts Pharaoh's servants bowing to him and asking the departure of the people he leads, then leaves in anger. The worship/bowing verb has a human recipient here; bow avoids imposing a religious sense solely from the verb.

Pharaoh will not listen to the plural you, so God's signs and wonders are greatly multiplied. Greatly renders the cognate multiplication emphasis; the two categories remain explicit in this Greek reading.

The brothers perform all the signs and wonders before Pharaoh; the Lord hardens his heart and he refuses Israel's departure. This summary preserves both divine action and Pharaoh's unwillingness without blending their grammatical roles.
The Lord speaks to both Moses and Aaron in Egypt. The location is explicit and anchors the following calendar and ritual commands before the departure narrative.
The present month becomes the beginning and first of the year's months for the addressees. No month name or modern calendar equivalent is supplied by the selected clause.

The tenth-day instruction apportions one animal by ancestral household and then by house. The flock-animal noun is broad enough to include the goat option expressly permitted in 12:5; propose animal from the flock rather than species-restrictive sheep, retaining the repeated one-per-house structure.

A small household combines with its nearest neighbour according to the number of persons and each one's sufficient portion. Use animal from the flock consistently with 12:3 and the sheep-or-goat alternatives in 12:5; the reckoning is by consumption capacity, not an invented fixed group size.

The animal must be unblemished, male and one year old, and may be taken from lambs or young goats. Replace Your sheep with Your animal from the flock so the opening noun does not contradict the explicit goat category; retain and as the source's coordination of the available groups.

The animal is kept until the fourteenth day and slaughtered by the whole assembly toward evening. Toward evening follows the selected Greek timing and does not import a more precise between-two-evenings formula.

Blood is placed on both doorposts and the lintel of the houses where the animals are eaten. The plural object them is natural in the distribution across households, even after the representative singular animal.

The night's food consists of fire-roasted meat and unleavened bread with bitter herbs. The preparation terms and accompanying bitterness remain concrete; no symbolic explanation is added to the food instructions.

Raw and water-boiled preparation are prohibited; fire-roasting includes head, feet and inner parts. The body-part list is retained without adding a butchery reconstruction that the verse does not state.

Nothing remains until morning, no bone is broken, and any remnant is burned. The bone prohibition is explicitly present here in this Greek text as well as in 12:46; repetition must not be removed as a suspected duplication.

Girded loins, sandals and staffs mark readiness, and eating is with haste. The final Passover-to-the-Lord identification remains a ritual designation; the borrowed name itself does not settle the etymological explanation.

God passes through Egypt, strikes firstborn humans and livestock, and executes vengeance against Egyptian gods. The universality of the listed divine targets and the closing Lord identification are both retained.

Blood is a sign on the occupied houses; God sees it and shelters the people from destructive plague. Shelter follows the selected covering verb rather than automatically rendering every related passage as pass over.

The day becomes a memorial and recurring feast through all generations under a perpetual statute. The repeated celebrate language supports an ongoing institution without adding a modern schedule beyond the stated day.

Seven days of unleavened bread require removal of leaven from the first day; eating it brings destruction from Israel. Soul denotes the person subject to the sanction here, not an independently specified immaterial component.

The first day is called holy and the seventh is a holy appointed day; servile work is forbidden except preparation for each person. The exact gathering force of the seventh-day adjective and the implied food scope of the exception require review; the source does not explicitly name food in this clause.

The people must keep this commandment because God will bring their host out on this day. Commandment is the selected object rather than an inserted unleavened-bread term; the future exodus and perpetual observance are distinct.

Unleavened eating runs from the evening associated with the fourteenth day of the first month to the evening of the twenty-first. Both endpoint dates and evening qualifications are retained without imposing a modern calendar conversion.

Seven days without household leaven apply to both the resident stranger and native; eating leavened food triggers removal from Israel's assembly. The source's different stranger term here and in 12:48 warrants glossary review without implying that all stranger categories are interchangeable.

The prohibition covers anything leavened, while unleavened food is required in every dwelling. The verse's parallel negative and positive commands are preserved rather than merged into a single dietary summary.

Moses gathers the entire elders' council and tells families to take the Passover animal. Propose animal from the flock instead of sheep, following the same inclusive noun and the lamb-or-young-goat eligibility of 12:5; slaughter remains the concrete ritual action.

Hyssop is dipped in blood beside the door and applied to lintel and both posts, with no one leaving until morning. Beside the door is the selected location; a basin is not inserted from another textual form.

The Lord passes through to strike, sees the marked doorway, passes by it and prevents the destroyer from entering. The Lord and destroying agent are grammatically distinguished, while the latter is not expressly called an angel in this verse.

The plural command to keep the word shifts to singular yourself and your sons in the enduring statute. Ordinary English you permits the distributive address, but the number change should be recorded in later full alignment.

Entry into the promised land is the future circumstance for maintaining this service. When is idiomatic English for the expected conditional arrival; it does not remove the command's dependence on that entry.
The anticipated sons' question asks what this service is. It begins an open exchange completed in 12:27, without adding to you to the question where the chosen Greek does not express it.

The reply identifies a Passover sacrifice and God's sheltering of Israel's houses while striking Egypt and rescuing ours. Shelter and rescue remain distinct verbs; the people's bowing then resumes narration outside the quoted explanation.
Israel goes and does as commanded to Moses and Aaron, with a repeated so they did formula. Keeping the repetition preserves the compliance emphasis rather than treating it as accidental duplication.

At midnight the blow ranges from Pharaoh's firstborn to that of a captive woman in the pit and livestock firstborn. The captive is explicitly feminine in this selected Greek; male prisoner or mill servant would change this fulfillment account.

Pharaoh, attendants and all Egyptians rise at night amid a great cry because every house has someone dead. The strong universal house statement is preserved without adding a proposed demographic explanation.

Pharaoh summons both brothers by night and releases them together with Israel to serve their God as requested. The repeated you and sons of Israel includes the leaders and community instead of restricting release to the negotiators.

Sheep and cattle are now allowed to go, and Pharaoh asks a blessing for himself also. This directly reverses the livestock reservation in 10:24; the request remains his speech rather than a reported blessing already given.

The Egyptians urgently press for expulsion, explaining that they are all dying. The present-tense cry conveys their fear and experience, not an external narrator's statement that every Egyptian subsequently died.

The people carry unleavened dough, with kneaded batches bound in garments on their shoulders. The selected material noun refers to the batches themselves; kneading bowls would insert containers not named in the Greek.

Israel follows Moses' instruction and asks for silver articles, gold articles and clothing. Asking is retained without a euphemistic borrowing verb being inserted at this point; the lending report comes next.

The Lord grants favour, Egyptians lend to Israel, and Israel plunders them. The apparent tension is part of the selected narrative wording; no repayment, coercion mechanism or reconciliation is invented.

The departure is from Rameses to Succoth with about six hundred thousand male pedestrians besides the household company. The approximate expression and male noun are explicit; household company represents the collective dependents term rather than a second counted army.

A substantial mixed company accompanies the departure, along with sheep, cattle and abundant livestock. The group's precise ethnic composition is not specified by the adjective and is not supplied in the translation.

The dough becomes unleavened hearth-cakes because expulsion prevented waiting and journey provisioning. Hearth-cakes preserves the preparation image provisionally; the verse does not specify a modern oven or recipe.

The four hundred and thirty years include residence in both Egypt and Canaan in this selected Greek. Neither location may be deleted to fit another chronology, and no extra ancestral clause is supplied from an unconsulted witness.
After the four hundred and thirty years all the Lord's host leaves Egypt. The inherited wording correctly omits an additional selfsame-day phrase not present in this running-text verse.

The night is described as a vigil for the Lord connected with bringing Israel out, then as an enduring vigil for Israel. The repeated watch noun and dative relationship are difficult; retain the inherited wording provisionally without deciding whether the first vigilance is primarily God's or the people's.

The Passover law excludes the outsider of another people. Foreigner here renders a different term from the resident newcomer later permitted under conditions; the apparent tension is not resolved by silently equating those statuses.

A household slave or silver-bought person must be circumcised before eating. Or is expressed in the selected Greek and is retained rather than silently merging the two descriptions into one exclusive purchase formula.

A sojourner or hired worker is excluded. The sojourner word differs from the incoming resident in 12:48; the exact social/legal relationship among those labels needs specialist review rather than a blanket modern citizenship analogy.

The meal stays in one house, meat is not taken outside, and no bone is broken. The bone rule intentionally repeats 12:10; preserving it makes no claim about later interpretation outside this OT scope.
The entire assembly of Israel is to perform the observance. The collective subject does not erase the household allocation and restrictions already stated in the surrounding instructions.

An incoming resident wishing to observe Passover must have every male belonging to him circumcised, then becomes like a native for this observance. The final blanket exclusion of the uncircumcised remains alongside the conditional admission.

One law applies to the local inhabitant and the incoming resident among them. The equality is stated within this legislative context, without adding an unexpressed universal proposition about every social status elsewhere.

Israel's obedience is reported with the command transmitted through Moses and Aaron and a repeated so they did. Concerning them conveys the final prepositional relationship without making the brothers the only observers.
The Lord brings Israel out that day with their host. Their belongs to Israel's collective force here, distinct from the Lord's host in 12:41; the possessives are not standardized.
The Lord's speech to Moses introduces the firstborn command in the next unit. The short formula is preserved separately to maintain the stored verse identity.

Consecration covers every firstborn opening a womb among Israel, human and animal, because it belongs to God. The paired firstborn descriptions retain the emphasis on initial offspring without inventing a second independent category.

Moses commands remembrance of the exodus from the house of slavery by the Lord's mighty hand, followed by the leaven prohibition. The bodily and household images remain, with no explanatory allegory inside the translation.
Departure occurs today in the month of new produce. Grain supplies the likely seasonal referent of the substantival new things; the Greek does not give a transliterated month name in this verse.

The promised territory lists seven peoples, including Girgashites, and is characterized by milk and honey. The oath to the fathers leads to observance in this month; the full list is retained rather than conformed to a shorter one.

The selected instruction says six days of unleavened eating followed by the seventh-day feast. Six must not be silently changed to seven to remove its difference from the next verse's seven-day summary.

Unleavened eating is now explicitly seven days, with neither leavened food nor leaven present throughout the territory. The two nouns and their separate prohibitions remain alongside the six-plus-one wording of 13:6.

The explanation to the son says because of this the Lord God acted for me during the departure. The demonstrative's causal direction is difficult; retain it without recasting the sentence as the familiar because of what the Lord did.

The observance becomes a hand sign and memorial before the eyes so the Lord's law is in the mouth. The command's imagery is retained without deciding from this verse alone its later material ritual implementation.

The law is kept at seasonally appointed times, with a days-to-days idiom rendered from year to year. That annual interpretation follows the month-and-feast context, not a claim that day always lexically means year.
Entry into Canaan and its gift fulfill the oath to the fathers and introduce the following dedication rule. The open temporal construction is preserved across the verse boundary.

Male womb-openers are set apart to the Lord, specifically from herds and other livestock born to the addressee. The repetition of male is intentional and is not broadened to every female firstborn animal.

A donkey's firstborn is exchanged for a sheep, and failure to exchange leads to redemption in this Greek text. Breaking its neck is not stated here. The flock-animal noun's exact permitted scope outside chapter 12 needs review; the human-firstborn redemption remains a separate command.

A son's later question receives the account of deliverance by the Lord's mighty hand from Egyptian slavery. Later is a temporal expression, not a precisely dated anniversary supplied by the translator.

Pharaoh's stubborn refusal is followed by firstborn deaths and the parent's explanation of animal sacrifice and human redemption. The death verb lacks an explicit subject here; inherited capitalized He identifies the Lord from context, a defensible but editorial resolution requiring review.

The sign is on the hand and something unshakable or fixed before the eyes, grounded in the exodus. Reminder supplies the contextual function from the parallel 13:9; it is not an additional explicit Greek noun in this clause.

God avoids the Philistine route, described as near, lest war cause the people to change their minds and return. The causal connection of nearness to the detour is retained as written; no explanatory map or imagined battle is added.

The detour leads toward the Red Sea, and Israel leaves in the fifth generation. The generation statement is explicit in the chosen Greek and must not be changed to armed or in ranks to match another textual reading.

Moses carries Joseph's bones under the oath Joseph imposed, with emphatic assurance that the Lord would visit. Lord is the title here; the quotation is not silently harmonized to another occurrence's divine title.

The journey proceeds from Succoth to the camp beside the wilderness at the place rendered Etham. The Greek form differs from the familiar English spelling; retain stable naming provisionally rather than claiming exact transliteration.

God leads by cloud in daytime to show the route and by fire at night. The selected wording here does not add a further purpose clause about traveling day and night, so the inherited concise form stands.

The cloud and fire pillars do not fail before all the people in their respective day and night periods. The repeated temporal pairing is preserved rather than treating the two descriptions as separate groups' guides.
The Lord speaks to Moses before the movement order. Preserve this introductory unit without attaching a destination not named until 14:2.

The people turn back and camp opposite a settlement between Migdol and the sea, facing Baal-zephon. Settlement follows the common noun in the Greek rather than importing a different proper place-name; the plural before them has an uncertain local referent and remains flagged.

Pharaoh will tell his own people that Israel wanders and the wilderness has enclosed them. The interpretation is attributed to Pharaoh and is not turned into the narrator's independent assessment of Israel's navigation.

Divine hardening leads to pursuit and glorification through Pharaoh and his entire army, then Egyptian recognition. The closing they did so returns to Israel's obedience to the camping order outside the divine speech.

News of flight changes Pharaoh's and his attendants' hearts; they regret losing Israel's service. The plural quotation preserves their shared complaint, while the first report leaves the messenger unnamed.

Pharaoh harnesses chariots in the plural and takes all his people with him. The selected plural should not be reduced to a single personal chariot, nor all his people recast as a precisely numbered army here.

The equipment includes six hundred chosen chariots, the Egyptian horse force and officers over all. The officers' term has an ancient chariot-related history, but its exact rank or crew function is not established in this review.

The Lord hardens Pharaoh's and his attendants' hearts; Pharaoh pursues while Israel departs with a high hand. The image is retained without resolving it exclusively to defiance, confidence or military armament.

The Egyptians find the camp beside the sea, with Pharaoh's horse force, chariots, riders and army located opposite the settlement and Baal-zephon. The varied military nouns and repeated geography are kept rather than standardized to cavalry alone.

Israel looks up as Pharaoh approaches and sees Egyptians camped behind them, then fears and cries to the Lord. Camped is the selected action, not the familiar marching after them wording from another tradition.

The people's sarcastic tomb question accuses Moses of bringing them to death in the wilderness, followed by a second accusation. The singular speech verb can take the collective people as subject; natural English they does not identify an extra speaker.

They recall their own alleged request to remain serving Egypt and prefer that to dying in this wilderness. The quoted recollection is not silently treated as a separately narrated earlier event in this chapter.

Moses commands courage, standing and sight of God's salvation for us today. Us includes Moses in the community, while the no-more-seeing claim is qualified by as you have seen them today; both features are maintained.
The Lord will fight on their behalf while they keep silent. The future silence clause is retained without turning the verse into a promise that no human action will ever be commanded in the crossing.
The Lord's singular question addresses Moses' cry, then orders Israel to set out. The shift from Moses to the whole people is important after the collective cry in 14:10.

The command has an unusual raise-with-your-staff construction followed by extending the hand, splitting the sea and Israel's entry on dry ground. The inherited opening is awkward English; retain provisionally and flag the dative/instrumental syntax rather than silently pretending the source has an uncomplicated accusative staff object.

The threatened hardening now includes Pharaoh and all Egyptians, who enter after Israel. Glory is specified through Pharaoh, army, chariots and horses; the widened subject group is not reduced to Pharaoh alone.
All Egyptians recognize the Lord in the glorification through Pharaoh, chariots and horses. This verse's list omits the army noun present in 14:17, and no harmonizing repetition is supplied.

God's angel moves from the front to the rear, and the cloud pillar also moves behind. The parallel movements are both explicit; their precise ontological relation is not resolved by merging the two subjects.

The intervening presence brings darkness and gloom, the night passes, and the camps do not mingle. This chosen Greek does not say the cloud illuminates one side; that familiar feature is not imported.

Moses stretches his hand, and the Lord drives the sea with a violent south wind all night, producing dry sea and divided water. South is the selected direction and must not be changed to east for geographic harmonization.
Israel enters on dry ground with water as a wall on the right and a wall on the left. Repeated wall is the source's balanced image and should not be compressed away solely for stylistic variety.
Egypt pursues into the sea with Pharaoh's horse force, chariots and riders. The plural English horses realizes the collective noun, while riders remains distinct from chariots.
During the morning watch the Lord looks upon Egypt's camp in the fire-and-cloud pillar and disorders it. The temporal watch is retained without an unsupported modern clock-hour conversion.

God binds the chariot axles and drives them with force; the Egyptians urge flight because the Lord fights for Israel. Bound axles is the selected wording, not removed wheels, and the force/difficulty nuance remains a translation question.
The hand command calls the water to return and cover Egyptians, chariots and riders. The water's two commanded actions are preserved without adding a new wind change not stated here.

At daybreak the water returns to its place, Egyptians flee beneath it, and the Lord shakes them into the sea. Beneath is the selected directional phrase; a familiar toward it is not substituted to smooth the difficult scene.

The returning water covers chariots, riders and the whole force that entered after Israel, leaving none. The relative clause defines the destroyed group; the verse is not expanded into a claim about every Egyptian everywhere.
Israel's dry-ground passage and the two water walls are repeated in contrast to Egypt's fate. The repetition is narrative emphasis and remains rather than being removed as already described.
The Lord rescues Israel from Egypt's hand, and Israel sees dead Egyptians on the shore. The bodily power image and the visible aftermath are retained as distinct statements.

Israel sees the great divine hand in what was done, fears the Lord and trusts both God and His attendant Moses. The shared trust construction does not erase the servant relationship or make the two objects equivalent in status.

Moses and Israel sing to God, then invite Let us sing to the Lord, a first-person plural exhortation. The glory cognate and horse/rider image recur in 15:21; retain the inherited poetry breaks and do not substitute a singular I will sing.

Helper and shelter describe the one who becomes salvation for the singer, followed by my God and my father's God. The inherited opening represents a difficult predicate sequence; preserve it provisionally without replacing the source's helper/shelter pair with strength and song.
The Lord is described as shattering wars, and Lord is His name. This selected image is not the man-of-war formula of another tradition; no military human noun should be inserted.

Pharaoh's chariots and host are cast into the sea, and chosen riders/officers are submerged in the Red Sea. The compact apposition of riders and officers needs fuller military terminology review; the poem's lineation is preserved.

God covers them with sea, then they sink like a stone into the depth. Sea is instrumental in the first clause, while the plural people share the singular stone comparison; no grammar correction to stones is needed.

Two right-hand clauses address the Lord and describe glorification in strength and shattered enemies. Thy marks the divine addressee, but has agrees with the third-person subject hand; changing it to hast would be ungrammatical.

Abundant divine glory shatters opponents, and the sent wrath consumes them like stubble. The two images and direct divine address remain; the wrath's consuming agency is personified without adding a literal fire noun.

The breath of divine wrath parts water, which becomes fixed like a wall, with waves fixed in the sea's midst. Stood fast is a provisional idiomatic rendering of the stiffening verb; no physical freezing mechanism is asserted.

The enemy's first-person boasts progress through pursuit, capture, spoil, satisfaction, sword-killing and dominion. Fill my soul preserves the appetite/self image without replacing it with a new emotional motive; ordinary my belongs to the enemy, not the divine addressee.

God sends His wind, the sea covers the enemy, and they sink like lead in powerful waters. Wind is the contextual sense here, distinct from breath of wrath in 15:8; the common Greek noun does not require one English gloss everywhere.

The questions compare the Lord among gods and as glorified among holy ones, wondrous in glories and performing wonders. Holy ones is a masculine reading of a form also permitting a neuter holy-things/places interpretation; that ambiguity requires review rather than an automatic in holiness substitution.
The outstretched divine right hand is followed by earth swallowing the enemy. Retain earth despite the preceding sea imagery; replacing it with sea would smooth away the poem's chosen image.

Guidance is in righteousness, not an imported mercy term; redemption identifies the guided people. The second verb can concern calling, encouragement or comfort, and its movement toward a holy dwelling makes inherited comfort them to awkward; retain provisionally with explicit lexical/syntax review pending.

The nations hear and become angry, while pangs seize Philistia's inhabitants. Angry follows the selected verb rather than a familiar trembled rendering; the birth-pain image of pangs remains distinct.

Edom's leaders hasten, Moab's rulers are seized by trembling, and Canaan's inhabitants melt. The first verb states haste rather than automatically the same fear as the second clause; all three contrasting images remain.

Fear and trembling are wished upon the peoples, followed by an imperative to become stone until God's acquired people pass. The optative and command are preserved as prayer rather than converted into past narrative; purchased is a provisional acquisition sense without an invented payment.

The song petitions God to bring and plant the people in His inheritance mountain and prepared dwelling. The imperative is important: this is not merely a future prediction, and the repeated Lord address and sanctuary apposition retain their line structure.
The Lord's reign extends through age, upon age and still further. For ever and ever, and beyond retains the extended duration formula without adding a specific historical endpoint.

The explanatory prose contrasts Pharaoh's horses, chariots and riders entering the sea with Israel's dry-ground walking. The collective horse noun is naturally plural; the Lord remains the agent bringing the waters upon the pursuing force.

Miriam is explicitly prophetess and Aaron's sister, carrying a timbrel and leading all the women with instruments and dances. The female designation and participation are preserved without an added restriction on her prophetic role.

Miriam leads the group in the same first-person plural singing invitation and horse/rider refrain as 15:1. The leadership verb supports led in song; the inherited poetry breaks preserve the refrain's two clauses.

Moses leads Israel onward from the Red Sea into Shur, followed by three days without finding drinkable water. The stated inability concerns finding water to drink, not an invented claim that no water of any sort existed anywhere.

The arrival name is Marah, but its explanatory designation is translated Bitterness because the water cannot be drunk. Keeping both the proper-name form and the translated explanation preserves the source's wordplay presentation.
The people murmur against Moses and ask what they will drink. The collective subject's singular verb and plural quoted question are natural together; no separate rebel spokesman is named.

Moses cries, the Lord shows wood, and its casting sweetens the water. The following ordinances and testing use singular him without a newly named recipient; inherited divine capitalization identifies the appointing subject, while whether him refers to Moses or corporate Israel remains unresolved.

The condition combines diligent hearing, pleasing action, attention to commands and keeping ordinances, followed by exemption from Egyptian diseases and God's healing identity. The shift from third-person Lord to divine first person is retained rather than editorially flattened to one speech perspective.

Elim has twelve water springs and seventy palm trunks, and the people camp by the waters. Trunks follows the expressed plant-part noun; the exact numbers remain, without adding a symbolic tribal interpretation.
